Family Health

Breast cancer radiotherapy: treatment, schedules and side effects

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Being offered radiotherapy can raise practical questions as well as worries about radiation: why is it needed after surgery, what will a session feel like, and can you still be close to your family? For breast cancer, the answer depends on the treatment area and purpose. Understanding the plan helps you discuss the expected benefit, prepare for appointments and recognize problems that need support.

What radiotherapy does

Radiotherapy uses high-energy radiation to damage cancer cells so that they die or stop growing. It treats a planned area rather than circulating through the whole body like a systemic medicine. Nearby healthy tissue can also be affected, which is why treatment planning and monitoring matter.

The aim is not simply to use the lowest possible dose or to make treatment last as long as possible. The team selects a dose, number of sessions and technique that balance cancer control with effects on healthy tissues. Some changes recover after treatment; others can persist or appear later.

Why it may be recommended after surgery

After breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy commonly reduces the risk of cancer returning in the breast or nearby regions. After a mastectomy, it may still be needed because risk is not determined only by whether the breast has been removed. The original tumour, lymph nodes and tissue margins all contribute to the decision.

Examples that can favour treatment after mastectomy include involved lymph nodes, a large tumour (such as one over five centimetres) or cancer at relevant surgical margins. These examples are not a rule you should apply alone. Ask how your pathology, any treatment before surgery and overall health affect the recommendation, including whether omission is an appropriate option.

Other treatment goals and combinations

Radiotherapy can also target a site where breast cancer has spread, such as a painful bone lesion or disease in the brain. In that setting the aim may be symptom relief, local control or prevention of a particular complication. That is a different discussion from reducing recurrence after surgery for early disease.

The plan may involve surgery, chemotherapy, hormone treatment or targeted medicines as well. Ask what each treatment contributes and in what order it will happen. A recommendation for one site does not mean radiation will treat every cancer cell elsewhere in the body.

External-beam treatment: which area receives radiation?

External-beam radiotherapy comes from a machine outside the body. Depending on the operation and cancer findings, the target can include the whole breast, only part of the breast, the chest wall or selected lymph-node areas. A boost is an additional dose focused on the area where the tumour was removed.

Partial-breast treatment is an option for selected early cancers rather than a suitable shortcut for everyone. Tumour features, margins, lymph nodes and other risk factors matter. Radiation may approach the target from several directions; the visible movement of the machine is part of delivering the planned treatment.

The consultation and planning scan

Before treatment, the radiation oncology team reviews your medical history, surgery, pathology and other therapies. You can ask about the expected benefit and both common and uncommon risks. Tell them about previous radiotherapy, an implanted device such as a pacemaker, breastfeeding, or any possibility of pregnancy before scans or treatment.

A planning scan maps the area and nearby organs. Staff help you find a position that can be repeated, often using an arm support or breast board. Small tattoos, temporary skin marks or other positioning systems may be used. Follow the team’s instructions for markings; if they fade, ask for help rather than redrawing them yourself.

Staying comfortable and protecting nearby organs

Tell the team if a shoulder is stiff, lying flat hurts, or anxiety makes it difficult to remain still. Supports and an individualized approach can help. Planning is also an opportunity to practise any breathing instructions rather than discovering them during the first treatment.

For some breast or lymph-node treatments, especially on the left side, a deep-inspiration breath hold moves the heart farther from the treatment area. Staff coach and monitor this. If you cannot comfortably perform a breath hold, tell them; other planning approaches can be considered. It is not a test of effort.

What an external-beam session feels like

Positioning and safety checks usually take longer than the radiation delivery itself, which is often only a few minutes. The machine may make noises or move around you, but the radiation is not something you feel entering the breast. Discomfort from the position should still be reported.

Staff step outside during delivery and watch and communicate with you from the control area. Ask how to signal if you need a pause. Most people attend as outpatients. External-beam treatment does not leave a radioactive source in your body, so it does not make ordinary contact with children or other family members unsafe.

Brachytherapy: radiation from a temporary source

Brachytherapy places a radiation source close to the area being treated. For selected people after breast-conserving surgery, it can deliver partial-breast treatment around the surgical cavity. Suitability depends on the cancer and anatomy; it is not automatically a safer replacement for treating the whole breast.

One approach uses a catheter with a balloon-like device in the cavity; another uses several small catheters through the tissue. Placement is a procedure in its own right, so discuss anaesthesia, pain relief and care of the insertion sites. The radioactive source can travel through the device for treatment and then be withdrawn while the catheter remains for later sessions.

How long will treatment take?

Start dates depend on healing, chemotherapy and the rest of the cancer plan. A fixed promise to start three or four weeks after every operation is misleading. Ask for a calendar that includes planning, treatment and any boost, and tell the team about transport, work or caring responsibilities that could make attendance difficult.

Many modern courses are shorter than older schedules. For example, NICE guidance includes five treatments over one week for appropriate breast or chest-wall treatment without regional lymph-node irradiation, with longer courses for some circumstances. Fifteen treatments over three weeks is another established option. The best schedule depends on the area and individual situation; fewer visits do not necessarily mean less effective care.

Understanding fractionation and internal-treatment schedules

A fraction is one treatment dose. Hypofractionation uses a larger dose per visit with fewer visits. Hyperfractionation means smaller doses more than once a day. Accelerated treatment shortens the overall elapsed course. These terms describe scheduling concepts, not a menu from which to choose a regimen yourself.

Brachytherapy timing varies too. A high-dose-rate source may be present for minutes at a time and removed between sessions; some other techniques keep a source in place longer and require different precautions. Do not assume every breast course is twice daily for five days: current ASTRO partial-breast guidance favours daily or alternate-day schedules over twice-daily courses. Get the actual plan and restrictions from your service.

Common short-term effects

During or after external treatment, you may notice tiredness, breast tenderness, swelling or a feeling of heaviness. Treated skin can become itchy, dry, red, darker or otherwise different from its usual colour. Some areas may peel or become sore, especially where skin rubs against skin.

Symptoms do not always end on the last treatment day. They can persist or briefly worsen before settling, and the recovery pattern varies. Hair loss from radiation is mainly limited to the treated area: breast treatment can affect underarm hair, but usually does not cause scalp hair loss. Other treatments may have different effects.

Effects that deserve longer-term discussion

Breast size, texture or firmness may change, and some swelling can last. Treatment may affect milk production in the treated breast and the outcome of reconstruction. Radiation to lymph-node regions can contribute to lymphoedema, a persistent swelling that needs assessment and management.

Less common late effects can involve the ribs, nerves, lung or heart; a later radiation-associated cancer is very rare. Modern planning reduces exposure but cannot remove every risk. Brachytherapy has its own possible effects, including bruising, pain, infection, fat-tissue damage and fluid collections, with rib injury uncommon. Comparing treatments requires your actual expected risks, not a blanket claim that internal treatment has fewer effects.

Care for the treated skin

Ask which products and washing methods your department recommends. Gentle washing, patting dry and a suitable moisturiser can help; avoid rubbing, tight clothing, perfume or products that irritate the area. Do not place heating pads, ice or unapproved adhesive dressings on treated skin. Protect the area from sun and avoid tanning beds.

A universal ban on deodorant is not necessary for everyone: some guidance allows a usual product if it does not irritate intact skin. Your team may give different instructions for broken skin or the timing of applications. Report peeling, wet or open areas, worsening soreness or possible infection rather than adding a home remedy. Special dressings or medicines may be needed.

Manage fatigue and know whom to call

Plan rest alongside gentle activity as tolerated, regular food and fluids, and help with tasks that are wearing you out. A brief note about when fatigue is worst and what it prevents you doing can make the next appointment more useful. Persistent exhaustion should be discussed; it should not simply be dismissed as something everyone must tolerate.

Get the team’s contact details and instructions for evenings or weekends. Report increasing pain, fever, new arm swelling, a new cough or breathlessness, and catheter-site redness or discharge if you have brachytherapy. Severe breathlessness or chest pain needs urgent medical assessment. Tell staff promptly if pregnancy becomes possible during the treatment course.

Leave with a follow-up and family-contact plan

After temporary brachytherapy, radiation precautions depend on whether a source is actually still present. Once that source has been removed, it is no longer emitting radiation from your body. A catheter alone is not a radioactive source. If a different implant method is planned, ask for written, method-specific advice about visitors and home contact.

Before the course ends, confirm when your next review is, which symptoms to keep reporting and who coordinates imaging and other cancer treatment. Ask about returning to work, exercise, sexual comfort, reconstruction and future feeding plans when relevant. A clear follow-up plan is part of treatment, not an optional extra once the machine appointments finish.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Breast radiotherapy is selected according to treatment goals, pathology, surgery and the areas at risk. Contemporary guidance supports shorter courses and partial-breast approaches for appropriate patients, but eligibility and schedules differ.

External treatment and internal sources have different procedures and contact precautions. Side effects can be temporary, persistent or delayed; planning, symptom monitoring and an individualized skin-care plan remain important.

How BeMama can help

Bring a written list of practical concerns to planning: travel, lifting or caring for children, work, shoulder comfort and whom to call. Ask the team to explain both the treatment benefit and the follow-up plan in your own situation.

When to seek help

Do not change or skip the prescribed schedule without talking to the team. Report worsening skin problems, fever, swelling or respiratory symptoms, and seek urgent care for severe breathlessness or chest pain.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Radiotherapy treats a planned area and can serve different goals at different cancer stages.
  • The treatment field and modern schedule are individualized; longer is not automatically better.
  • External-beam treatment does not make you radioactive.
  • Brachytherapy requires its own procedure, device-care and source-specific precautions.
  • Ask about common symptoms, late effects and a clear follow-up contact plan.

Frequently asked questions

Why would I need radiation after a mastectomy?

Some cancer features leave a meaningful risk in the chest wall or nearby nodes despite removal of the breast. Lymph nodes, tumour size, margins and the response to earlier treatment help guide the decision.

Is a one-week course too short to work?

Not necessarily. Evidence-based five-session schedules suit many situations. Other treatment areas or personal factors may favour a longer course. Ask why your particular schedule was chosen.

What does a boost mean?

It is an additional dose focused on the tumour bed, usually after breast-conserving surgery when the recurrence risk warrants it. It may be delivered during or after the main course.

Will I feel the radiation during a session?

Usually you will not feel the radiation itself. Positioning can still be uncomfortable, so tell staff if you need help or a pause. They can see and communicate with you during treatment.

Can I hold my child after external radiotherapy?

External-beam radiotherapy does not make you radioactive. Any restrictions on lifting would relate to surgery, comfort or another part of your care, not radiation being transferred by contact.

Is internal radiation always the safer option?

No. It is suitable for selected cases and carries procedure-related and tissue risks. Compare the expected benefits and harms of the options that actually fit your cancer.

Is every brachytherapy course twice a day for five days?

No. Schedules vary, and contemporary partial-breast guidance favours daily or alternate-day courses over twice-daily regimens. Follow the written plan from your radiation oncology team.

Will breast radiation make my scalp hair fall out?

Not usually. Radiation-related hair loss mainly occurs in the treated area, which can include the underarm for breast treatment. Some chemotherapy medicines can cause scalp hair loss.

Must I stop every deodorant or moisturiser?

Ask your service about suitable products and when to apply them. Some can be used on intact skin if they do not irritate it. Broken, wet or very sore skin needs a specific care plan.

Do symptoms always disappear when treatment ends?

No. Some peak after the final session, some take longer to settle, and some changes can persist or develop later. Keep follow-up appointments and report new or worsening symptoms.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
